whatItDoes: Allow Eaton to borrow $5 million for street and transportation improvements, with total repayment capped at $7.9 million. The measure does not impose a new tax or raise an existing rate. Repayment could use any legally available town revenue, including the 1% transportation sales and use tax approved in 2023. Listed projects include 10 th Street between Highway 85 and Christensen Avenue, Christensen Avenue north of East Collins Street, and South Cheyenne Avenue south of Collins Street. Borrowing could also pay issuance costs and reserves. The town could refinance within the same repayment cap and set an early-repayment charge no higher than 3%. Investment earnings on borrowed money could be kept and spent outside the stated revenue limits.
yesMeans: Authorize the street and transportation borrowing, repayment from existing town revenues and the investment-earnings revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not authorize this borrowing or its proposed investment-earnings revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Extend Kersey’s existing 17.205-mill property tax for 10 years, from 2028 through 2037, at the current rate. Revenue would continue paying for town operations and services. The extension would also approve exceptions to Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and the statutory property-tax revenue limit cited in the question.
yesMeans: Extend the current property tax through 2037 with the stated revenue-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not extend the tax beyond its currently authorized term or approve these proposed exceptions.

whatItDoes: Broaden the permitted uses of Evans’s existing sales tax on food bought for home consumption, without increasing the rate. Additional uses would include operating city facilities and performance-based economic-development incentives. Maintaining improvements previously financed by this tax, including the police facility, would remain the first priority. All spending would need city council approval and an appropriation. The measure would allow the tax revenue and investment earnings to be collected and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other stated legal limits.
yesMeans: Approve the broader permitted uses and the proposed revenue-limit exception, at the current tax rate.
noMeans: Keep the existing permitted uses of this tax and do not approve the proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Increase Frederick’s sales and use tax rate by 1 percentage point beginning January 1, 2027. It is expected to raise about $3.8 million in the first full collection year, followed by whatever the tax produces later. Money would be restricted to streets, alleys and related transportation infrastructure, including maintenance, intersections, paving and widening, sidewalks, transportation networks, and regional projects such as Highway 52 and frontage roads. Tax revenue and interest could be kept and spent outside the constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits identified in the measure.
yesMeans: Approve the additional transportation sales and use tax and the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve this additional tax or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Allow Frederick to borrow up to $26 million through general-obligation bonds for street and transportation construction projects, with total repayment capped at $57 million. This borrowing depends on voters also approving a 1 percentage-point increase in the sales and use tax. The town board would set the timing, sale prices, maturity and early-repayment terms of the bonds.
yesMeans: Authorize the transportation bonds within the borrowing and repayment caps, if the sales and use tax increase is also approved.
noMeans: Do not authorize these transportation bonds through this measure.

whatItDoes: Increase Greeley’s sales and use tax rate by 0.6 percentage points, or 60 cents on a $100 taxable purchase. The city’s sales tax on food would not increase. The measure would authorize $20 million in additional taxes for 2027 collection and the amount collected in each later year, for the specified civic, recreation and service projects. The tax would end when financing for both the downtown Civic Campus and West Greeley Catalyst projects, including refinancing, is fully repaid, and no later than December 31, 2067. A citizens committee would independently review spending. The measure would also authorize the financing commitments and revenue-limit exception described below.
yesMeans: Approve the additional project tax, its financing commitments, citizen review and revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve this additional tax or the financing authority proposed in this measure.

parts.label: Restricted uses
parts.what: Money could pay to finance, design, build, improve, operate and maintain the downtown Civic Campus, including city hall, a public plaza and parking garage; the West Greeley Catalyst project, including an arena, youth ice center, water park and hotel; recreational, cultural and service facilities; and city parks, playgrounds, pools, trails and other outdoor spaces, with related infrastructure and amenities.

parts.label: Multi-year financing
parts.what: The city could pledge this tax revenue to financing for any listed project through obligations lasting more than one fiscal year. It could also pledge other city revenue from the Catalyst project to that project’s financing. Tax receipts and their investment earnings could be kept and spent outside the constitutional and other legal revenue limits specified in the question.

whatItDoes: Increase Eaton School District’s taxes by up to $3,686,000 starting in 2026 for collection in 2027. In later years, the additional annual amount, combined with other locally approved school-funding amounts under the cited law, could not exceed 25% of the district’s total program funding. Money would go to the general fund for educational purposes, including career and technical learning, teacher and staff salaries, school resource officers and security systems. Tax revenue and its investment earnings could be kept and spent under the proposed exception to Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
yesMeans: Approve the additional school funding within the stated cap and the revenue-limit exception.
noMeans: Do not approve this additional tax authorization or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

whatItDoes: Increase Weld County School District RE-1’s property taxes by $1.3 million annually to fund recruiting, training and retaining teachers and staff through higher salaries and wages. The district would set the property-tax rate needed to raise that amount. Revenue would go to its general fund in addition to existing general-fund property taxes, as a voter-approved revenue change.
yesMeans: Approve the additional $1.3 million annual property-tax funding and the stated voter-approved revenue change.
noMeans: Do not approve this additional property-tax funding through this measure.

whatItDoes: Increase Prairie School District’s property taxes by $1,192,406 for 2027 collection. In later years, the annual amount would adjust so that it and previously approved additional local school taxes together equal 37% of the district’s total program funding, as defined by state law. Money would go to the general fund for recruiting, training and retaining teachers, salaries and wages for teachers and other school staff, and ongoing school-facility maintenance.
yesMeans: Approve the additional school property taxes, with future amounts adjusted to the combined 37% funding level.
noMeans: Do not authorize this additional property-tax funding through this measure.

whatItDoes: Increase Nunn Fire Protection District’s property-tax rate in three steps:1 additional mill in 2027, another 1 mill in 2028 and another 1 mill in 2029, for a total increase of 3 mills that continues afterward as allowed by law. The fully phased-in tax would raise up to $725,000 in 2029, followed by whatever additional amounts it produces later. Money would fund operating and capital expenses, including professional staffing, training, pay and benefits, vehicles, communications, protective gear and rescue equipment. The district could collect and spend this revenue outside the constitutional and statutory limits identified in the question.
yesMeans: Approve the phased-in property-tax increase and the proposed revenue and spending-limit exceptions.
noMeans: Do not approve this property-tax increase or its proposed limit exceptions.
